        if stop=='guard':raise RuntimeError('SYNTHETIC_GUARD_WITH_SAVED_NPZ')
        return m
    stub=types.ModuleType('replay_trial');stub.replay_trial=trial

full_later_report.absolute_output: the played signal sits at -42 to -47 dBFS, i.e. of order one percent of full scale, which is far too quiet to be heard clearly in a room regardless of the listener.
full_later_report.consistency_with_earlier_listener_record: every earlier "listener" record (2026-10-27 20 cm: no audible amplification; the same day: audible but not obviously louder; the talker-as-listener pair: cannot tell) is consistent with this measurement. what_would_change_it: a louder input (clipping: the ADC rails, and the v3 driver stops the run)
more digital gain (the zero arm is already 0.12 dB from its loudness peak at -8 dB, and -4 dB self-oscillates without cancellation)
a more efficient or closer speaker (not a parameter we control in this fixture)

listener_later_report.protocol: one quiet gate, then the same sentence in two 6 s windows (zero-coefficient arm, then the candidate arm, about 4 s apart). The talker was told BEFORE the run what to judge: which window is louder, whether there is howling, whether speech is intelligible. The first attempt asked for the judgement only after the run and was discarded as an invalid procedure, not as a result.

listener_later_report.reading: the microphone level drops 5.6 dB with cancellation active, but the person doing the speaking cannot hear that as a loudness difference. The likely reason is methodological: the talker is also the listener, so their own direct voice (bone conduction plus direct sound) dominates what they hear, and a change in the played level is masked. The historical sessions used a separate listener 20 cm from the speaker for exactly this reason.
listener_later_report.what_it_does_not_say: it does NOT say the cancellation is inaudible; it says this listener position cannot resolve it. A separate listener at the speaker, or a recorded A/B of the played signal, is needed to answer the audible-benefit question.
